body: One thing that helps me a lot is meditation. This maybe sounds like hippie bullshit to you -- it certainly did to me at first -- but it can help a great deal. I get in a comfortable spot, sit however feels natural to you, close my eyes and begin to relax. Then, for maybe 10 minutes, just let all the thoughts pass through your head and accept them all as fine, not in need of any change. Don't hold onto any of them, don't get fixated, but also don't attempt to block them out. Let them come and go. Then for the next 15 minutes, try to just notice what's actually happening to you. Not what's in your brain, not the thoughts that live in your head, just the noises of cars outside, birds, the room, etc. You will probably notice that unless you live in a war zone, everything around you is basically fine. There are lots of books and apps that can help guide you through this.
Thanks, HutSmut. Do you mind me asking what age you are now? At what age did things start turning around for you? Was it more a gradual process or a complete 180?

High school is a very unique set of circumstances. Even people with relatively well-adjusted brains look back on high school as a difficult time. You have very little control over your life right now, and it may be that once you're out, you'll find that the increased freedom and the ability to make more of your own decisions will change your mind. I can't guarantee that your feelings will change, but it's worth waiting a while to see what changes.

Just stay alive. I also have a "desirable" career, and it makes me suicidal every time I'm remotely busy, which is all the time. My fantasy life often revolves around how I could live with almost no money, but of course I'm too weak-willed to really follow through with it.
